lead: LU factorization writes a square matrix as A = LU, where L is unit lower triangular and U is upper triangular. It exists to avoid repeating Gaussian elimination for every right-hand side. Factor once, then solve two triangular systems for each new b. This is useful in circuit simulation, structural analysis, and any code that solves the same Ax = b with many b. Only a few universities teach this as an exam topic.
prereq: You need row operations and Gaussian elimination from 1.2 and 1.3.

blocks.text: For an n × n matrix A, write A = LU. L is unit lower triangular: 1s on the diagonal, zeros above it, and the elimination multipliers below it. U is upper triangular: zeros below the diagonal, and it is the echelon form after elimination. This is the Doolittle form. Crout form puts the pivots in L instead. The multiplier ℓ<sub>ik</sub> = a<sub>ik</sub>/a<sub>kk</sub> clears entry (i,k).

A = LU without row swaps works when every leading principal minor of A is nonzero: the determinants of the top-left 1×1, 2×2, ..., n×n blocks. If a zero pivot appears, swap rows: PA = LU, where P records the swaps.
The factors store the whole elimination history: U is the final staircase, and L records each row operation as a number. The product multiplies back to A exactly.

items: Copy A into U and make L the n × n identity matrix.
For k = 1 to n−1, use U[k][k] as the pivot; if it is 0, stop, because a row swap is needed.
For i = k+1 to n, set ℓ<sub>ik</sub> = U[i][k]/U[k][k] and store it in L[i][k].
For j = k to n, replace U[i][j] by U[i][j] − ℓ<sub>ik</sub>U[k][j].
After the last column, A = LU.

blocks.text: Store the multiplier before changing the row. The factorization costs about 2n<sup>3</sup>/3 operations. Each new right-hand side costs about 2n<sup>2</sup> operations for the two triangular solves, so reusing L and U is much cheaper than fresh elimination. No division by zero is allowed; a zero pivot stops the no-swap factorization.
To solve Ax = b, write LUx = b and set y = Ux. First solve Ly = b forward, from the top. Then solve Ux = y backward, from the bottom.

y<sub>i</sub> = b<sub>i</sub> − Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>i−1</sup> ℓ<sub>ij</sub>y<sub>j</sub>,   x<sub>i</sub> = (y<sub>i</sub> − Σ<sub>j=i+1</sub><sup>n</sup> u<sub>ij</sub>x<sub>j</sub>) / u<sub>ii</sub>
blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> is the forward-solve value; x<sub>i</sub> is the unknown; ℓ<sub>ij</sub> and u<sub>ij</sub> are entries of L and U; b<sub>i</sub> is the right-hand side.

blocks.text: The formulas use the top-to-bottom order for L and bottom-to-top order for U. The two solves are cheap and simple loops.

figure.caption: The factor step stores L and U once; each right-hand side then needs only a forward solve and a back solve.

spec.title: One factorization, two triangular solves
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow: Ax = b is factored as A = LU, then Ly = b is solved forward, Ux = y is solved backward, and x comes out.

examples.question: Factor A = [[2,1,1],[4,3,3],[8,7,9]] as A = LU, then solve Ax = b for b = (4,10,24).
steps: Start with U = A and L = I. Column 1 pivot is 2.
Row 2 multiplier: 4/2 = 2; row 2 becomes [0,1,1]. Row 3 multiplier: 8/2 = 4; row 3 becomes [0,3,5].
Column 2 pivot is 1. Row 3 multiplier: 3/1 = 3; row 3 becomes [0,0,2].
Back solve Ux = y = (4,2,2): 2x3 = 2 gives x3 = 1; x2+x3 = 2 gives x2 = 1; 2x1+x2+x3 = 4 gives x1 = 1.

traps: Putting multipliers in U instead of L; L must hold them below the diagonal.
Assuming every square matrix has A = LU with no row swap; a zero pivot needs PA = LU.
Forgetting the 1s on the diagonal of L.
Solving Ux = b before Ly = b; forward solve comes first.

quiz.q: In Doolittle form, what are the diagonal entries of L?
Why reuse L and U for many b?
quiz.a: Factorization is the costly part; each b needs only two O(n²) triangular solves.

quiz.q: A = [[0,1],[1,0]] is invertible. Does A = LU without row swaps exist?
quiz.a: No; first pivot is 0. Use PA = LU.
Ly = b gives y = (5,−1); Ux = y gives x = (11/6,−1/2).

quiz.q: Which condition guarantees no row swaps?
quiz.a: Every leading principal minor of A is nonzero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production libraries use partial pivoting and sparse LU for huge matrices from power grids and finite elements. Cholesky is the symmetric positive definite special case. Search 'LU with partial pivoting', 'sparse LU', and 'LAPACK getrf'.
